Sample sizes were small, few studies corrected for multiple testing, and athletes who did not return were not measured.",
 "synthesisCaution":"The 63% to 97% return range and the statement that most elite athletes returned to preinjury level may be read as an expected performance outcome for any athlete, when the performance data come from small, highly biased samples of elite players.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2017,
   "citation":"Mohtadi NG, Chan DS. Return to Sport-Specific Performance After Primary Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Systematic Review. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2017.",
   "doi":"10.1177/0363546517732541",
   "abstract":"This systematic review identified 15 prognostic studies of sport-specific performance after primary ACL reconstruction in competitive athletes and rated their risk of bias. Most high-level athletes returned to sport, the bulk of evidence showed a measurable decline in performance statistics that was highly sport-specific, and the literature was judged highly biased.",
   "tldr":"Many elite athletes return to sport after ACL reconstruction, but performance data are sparse, sport-specific and mostly biased. Expect a possible performance decline, not a fixed figure.",
   "methods":"Systematic review of Ovid MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane databases and PubMed, with hand searching of reference lists, for prognostic studies of sport-specific performance after primary ACL reconstruction. Two authors independently selected and extracted the studies, and each was rated on six QUIPS bias domains, with the overall rating based on participation, prognostic factor and confounding domains.",
   "findings":"Return to sport ranged from 63% (NFL players) to 97% (NHL players) across studies. Most studies reported no change or a decline in performance statistics after reconstruction, while three reported better performance in the ACLR group than in controls (hockey, soccer and alpine skiing). Most control-group comparisons favored the controls, but many lacked the numbers to show a difference and few corrected for multiple testing. Twelve of 15 studies were rated high risk of bias, mostly for how athletes were identified, and the two NHL studies reached different return and performance results depending on how injured players were found.",
   "limitations":"Only high-performance or professional athletes were studied, and no meta-analysis was possible because the outcomes and performance measures varied by sport. Most studies were small, did not correct for multiple testing, and used a case-control design that is closer to a retrospective cohort. Non-returning athletes were not measured, so performance among returners may be overstated.",
   "practicalImplications":"Staff counseling athletes about ACL reconstruction can say that many elite athletes return to sport, but that measured performance after return has generally declined or not changed, with large variation by sport. Because the data are biased, performance expectations should be presented as uncertain rather than as a fixed number.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: The review gives no performance benchmark for returning athletes, so programs can only use it to justify tracking sport-specific output before and after injury, which the authors themselves recommend.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: Most high-performance athletes returned to sport after ACL reconstruction (63% to 97%), but the review cannot show whether returners reach preinjury performance, because non-returners were not measured and the studies are rated highly biased. Return to sport alone should not be treated as evidence of a return to preinjury performance."
 },

   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[

     "populations: Mixed / Unspecified -> Male Athletes and Female Athletes added, since sex is stated per study (\"The majority of included individuals were males\"; WNBA and skier samples include females) and all samples are elite"
   ],

   "spotCheckPriority":"normal"
 }
}

8	 "identityCheck":"The title 'Return to Full Participation Following Concussion in the National Football League, 2015 Through 2020' in the text matches the filename.",
9	 "confidence":"high",

11	 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
12	 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Brain Health & Psychology","Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
13	 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Research & Analytics"],
14	 "sports":["American Football"],
15	 "populations":["Professional / Elite","Injured Athletes"],
16	 "evidenceSummary":"A retrospective cohort study of 1,480 team-related concussions in 1,121 NFL players across the 2015 to 2020 seasons, using electronic health record and league participation data. The median time missed was 9 days (mean 15.0), with an average of 3,639 player-days and 255 games lost per year, and 59% of players who were concussed in the regular season or preseason missed at least one game. No player returned to competition on the day of injury, and 37.7% of players concussed in a Sunday game played the following Sunday.",
17	 "screeningLimitations":"This is an observational study with no comparison group, and it does not measure symptom count, severity or neuropsychological test results, which the authors note predict return timing. Days and games were imputed for 8% and 13% of cases, and time lost depends on the timing of injury within the season and on roster decisions.",
18	 "synthesisCaution":"The 9-day median could be read as a recovery benchmark for any individual player, when it describes a league-wide protocol-driven timeline for professional football players and cannot predict one player's return.",
19	 "paper":{
20	   "year":2022,
21	   "citation":"Mack CD, Herzog MM, Solomon G, Putukian M, Lee RY, Matava MJ, et al. Return to Full Participation Following Concussion in the National Football League, 2015 Through 2020. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine. 2022.",
22	   "doi":"10.1097/JSM.0000000000001050",
23	   "abstract":"This retrospective cohort study quantified days missed, games missed and time to return to full participation after concussion in NFL players from 2015 to 2020. Players missed a median of 9 days, 59% missed at least one scheduled game, and no player returned on the day of injury.",
24	   "tldr":"NFL players missed a median of 9 days after a concussion, and about 59% missed at least one game. No player returned to competition on the day of injury under the league's graduated protocol.",
25	   "methods":"Retrospective observational cohort of team-related NFL concussions from 2015 to 2020, drawn from the league's electronic health record and participation data. Days missed, games missed and injury burden were summarized by year, season, activity, roster position and day of week, with Wilcoxon and Kruskal-Wallis tests for group comparisons.",
26	   "findings":"There were 1,480 concussions in 1,121 players. The median days missed was 9 (mean 15.0, SD 23.7), with an average of 3,639 player-days and 255 games missed per year. Offensive linemen (median 10 days), tight ends, running backs and linebackers missed the most days per concussion, and quarterbacks and special teams players missed the fewest. Practice and game concussions had similar median days missed (8 and 9, P = 0.40). Of players concussed in preseason or regular season games, 41% returned without missing a game, 37% after one game, and 22% after two or more.",
27	   "limitations":"The study has no comparison group and does not account for symptom severity, concussion history or neuropsychological results. Missing return dates were imputed for 8% of days and 13% of games, and time missed depends on when in the season the injury occurred and on roster decisions. The 2020 season was shortened by COVID-19, and the authors note that some concussions may go undetected.",
28	   "practicalImplications":"Staff planning for a concussed professional football player can use the median of about 9 days out and the likelihood of missing at least one game as a league-level benchmark. Clinical teams should not expect same-day return, since the league protocol prohibits it, and individual timelines should follow symptom-based progression.",
29	   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: Planning for a concussion absence in football should assume a median of about 9 days out of full participation and a substantial chance of missing a game. The paper measures no performance, workload or readiness data after return, so it cannot guide training loads once the player is back.",
30	   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: The league protocol requires graduated phases, symptom resolution and clearance by the team physician and an independent neurologist, with no same-day return. The study describes the outcome of that protocol but does not identify factors that predict longer recovery, so it cannot forecast an individual player's return date."
31	 }

1	   Original Research
2	
3	
4	
5	
6	Return to Full Participation Following Concussion in
7	the National Football League, 2015 Through 2020
8	Christina D. Mack, PhD, MSPH,* Mackenzie M. Herzog, PhD, MPH,* Gary Solomon, PhD,†‡ Margot Putukian, MD,
9	FACSM, FAMSSM,§ Rebecca Y. Lee, PhD,* Matthew J. Matava, MD,{ Javier Cárdenas, MD,k
10	Nicholas Theodore, MD,** and Allen Sills, MD‡
11	
12	
13	  Abstract
14	  Objective: Quantify days missed, games missed, injury burden, and time to return to full participation (RTFP) among National
15	  Football League (NFL) players who sustained a concussion. Design: Retrospective cohort study. Setting: 2015 through 2020
16	  NFL seasons. Participants: National Football League players diagnosed with a concussion from 2015 to 2020. Interventions:
17	  National Football League-mandated graduated RTFP protocol. Main Outcome Measures: Days missed, games missed,
18	  burden, and time to RTFP, overall and by position. Results: An annual average of 3639 player-days of participation and 255 games
19	  were missed across NFL because of concussion. Concussed players missed a median of 9 days (mean 5 15.0), a relatively stable
20	  metric over 6 years, with slight variation by position. Offensive linemen, tight ends, running backs, and linebackers missed the most
21	  days per concussion; defensive secondary, offensive linemen, and wide receivers sustained the highest injury burden. Post-
22	  concussion, 59% of players missed one or more scheduled games. Among players concussed in a Sunday game, 38% played in a
23	  Sunday game one week later. Conclusions: The 9-day median time missed post-concussion may be related to emphasis on
24	  graduated phase-based concussion management. No concussed player returned to competition on the day of injury, and less than
25	  40% participated in games the following week. Further work is needed to better understand characteristics of concussions that take
26	  longer to return and movement through stages of return.
27	  Key Words: American football, National Football League, concussion, epidemiology, return to play

Return to Full Participation Following Concussion in
the National Football League, 2015 Through 2020
Christina D. Mack, PhD, MSPH,* Mackenzie M. Herzog, PhD, MPH,* Gary Solomon, PhD,†‡ Margot Putukian, MD,
FACSM, FAMSSM,§ Rebecca Y. Lee, PhD,* Matthew J. Matava, MD,{ Javier Cárdenas, MD,k
Nicholas Theodore, MD,** and Allen Sills, MD‡


  Abstract
  Objective: Quantify days missed, games missed, injury burden, and time to return to full participation (RTFP) among National
  Football League (NFL) players who sustained a concussion. Design: Retrospective cohort study. Setting: 2015 through 2020
  NFL seasons. Participants: National Football League players diagnosed with a concussion from 2015 to 2020. Interventions:
  National Football League-mandated graduated RTFP protocol. Main Outcome Measures: Days missed, games missed,
  burden, and time to RTFP, overall and by position. Results: An annual average of 3639 player-days of participation and 255 games
  were missed across NFL because of concussion. Concussed players missed a median of 9 days (mean 5 15.0), a relatively stable
  metric over 6 years, with slight variation by position. Offensive linemen, tight ends, running backs, and linebackers missed the most
  days per concussion; defensive secondary, offensive linemen, and wide receivers sustained the highest injury burden. Post-
  concussion, 59% of players missed one or more scheduled games. Among players concussed in a Sunday game, 38% played in a
  Sunday game one week later. Conclusions: The 9-day median time missed post-concussion may be related to emphasis on
  graduated phase-based concussion management. No concussed player returned to competition on the day of injury, and less than
  40% participated in games the following week. Further work is needed to better understand characteristics of concussions that take
  longer to return and movement through stages of return.
  Key Words: American football, National Football League, concussion, epidemiology, return to play
  (Clin J Sport Med 2022;00:1–9)

4	 "decision":"INCLUDE",
5	 "exclusionReason":"",
6	 "degradedReason":"",
7	 "doiMissing":false,
8	 "identityCheck":"The title 'Return to performance: machine learning insights into how absence time following muscle injuries affects match running performance in LaLiga soccer players' in the text matches the filename.",
9	 "confidence":"high",
10	 "studyDesign":"Cohort Study",
11	 "primaryDomain":"Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
12	 "domains":["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport","Training & Performance","Sports Medicine & Injury"],
13	 "audiences":["Performance","Rehabilitation","Research & Analytics","Athletic Training"],
14	 "sports":["Soccer"],
15	 "populations":["Male Athletes","Professional / Elite","Injured Athletes"],
16	 "evidenceSummary":"A retrospective study of 110 lower-limb muscle injuries in 90 male LaLiga players during the 2022-2023 season, comparing four matches before and four after each injury. Mean absence was 34.6 days (SD 27.9). Maximal speed had the strongest negative correlation with absence time (r = -0.355), and maximal speed, maximal acceleration, time played and the composite index differed significantly after injury. Random forest and linear regression models explained 44% and 35% of variance in absence time on the test set (training-set R2 0.34 and 0.12).",
17	 "screeningLimitations":"The models were fitted on 110 injuries with an 80/20 split, so the test set is small, and the explained variance is modest. The study is observational and cannot separate absence effects from injury severity, tissue type, age or role, and no correction for multiple testing is reported. The paper also has a sign conflict: Table 3 gives a positive correlation for the maximal deceleration difference (r = 0.185), while the text describes deceleration declining with longer absence.",
18	 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the models as predicting how much speed or braking a given player will lose, when they explain only about a third to a half of the variance in absence time and show that longer absence goes with larger declines on average, not for each player.",
19	 "paper":{
20	   "year":2025,
21	   "citation":"Pecci J, Sánchez-Trigo H, Mancha-Triguero D, Sañudo B, Reverte-Pagola G, del Ojo-López JJ, et al. Return to performance: machine learning insights into how absence time following muscle injuries affects match running performance in LaLiga soccer players. Biology of Sport. 2025;42(4):275-286.",
22	   "doi":"10.5114/biolsport.2025.151651",
23	   "abstract":"This retrospective study of 110 muscle injuries in LaLiga players examined how absence time relates to changes in match running performance, using regression and random forest models. Maximal speed was the variable most strongly associated with longer absence, with maximal acceleration and deceleration also affected, while sprint count was not related to absence time.",
24	   "tldr":"Longer time out after a muscle injury goes with a larger drop in maximal speed, and to a lesser extent acceleration and braking, in match play. Sprint count did not follow absence time, so it should be checked regardless of how long a player was out.",
25	   "methods":"Retrospective design using match external-load data from the 2022-2023 LaLiga season, comparing four pre-injury and four post-injury matches for 110 lower-limb muscle injuries in 90 male players. Pre- and post-injury differences were tested with paired t-tests or Wilcoxon tests, then Pearson correlations with absence time were calculated, and multiple linear regression and random forest models with SHAP values were fitted to absence time using an 80/20 train-test split.",
26	   "findings":"Mean absence was 34.6 days (SD 27.9), with 51 hamstring injuries. Time played, total distance, maximal acceleration, maximal deceleration, maximal speed, sprint distance, relative sprint count and the composite index differed significantly after injury. Maximal speed fell by a mean of 0.48 km/h and showed the strongest correlation with absence (r = -0.355), followed by time played (r = -0.328) and maximal acceleration (r = -0.303). Test-set R2 was 0.348 for linear regression and 0.442 for random forest, and maximal speed was the top feature in both models. Relative sprint count had the weakest correlation with absence (r = -0.149).",
27	   "limitations":"The sample is 110 injuries from one season, with a small test set and modest explained variance, and the training-set linear model R2 was only 0.12. The design is observational, so absence time cannot be separated from injury severity, tendon involvement, age or playing role, and no correction for multiple testing is reported. Table 3 shows a positive correlation for the maximal deceleration difference (r = 0.185), which conflicts with the text's claim that deceleration declines with longer absence; the table values are reported here.",
28	   "practicalImplications":"After a muscle injury with a longer absence, staff should expect larger drops in match maximal speed and acceleration, so return-to-play criteria should include specific tests of maximal speed and acceleration or braking before clearance. Sprint count did not track absence time, so it should be checked regardless of how long the player was out.",
29	   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: Players returning after longer absences are likely to lose top speed and acceleration in matches, so reconditioning should include speed and acceleration work targeted at those outputs. The paper reports no load prescriptions, so volumes must come from elsewhere.",
30	   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: The study supports checking maximal speed, acceleration and deceleration before return to play, with more emphasis on those tests after longer absences. It cannot set a return date or a performance threshold for an individual player, and the authors' recommendation to check sprinting regardless of absence time also applies."
31	 }
32	}

ABSTRACT: To determine how absence time after muscle injuries affects external load metrics in elite soccer                Horacio Sánchez-Trigo
players and identify which performance variables are most impacted by the injury. A total of 110 lower limb                0000-0002-1830-8236
muscle injuries from LaLiga players were analysed. Following an analysis of pre- and post-injury data to identify          Borja Sañudo
which outcomes were affected by muscle injury, machine learning algorithms were employed to examine                        0000-0002-9969-9573
relationships between absence duration and performance metrics. Maximal speed, maximal acceleration, maximal               Gonzalo Reverte-Pagola
                                                                                                                           0000-0001-9396-6354
deceleration, composite index (i.e., overall player performance) and sprint count during matches were the most
                                                                                                                           Roberto López del Campo
affected variables after return to play. The multiple linear regression (MLR) model and random forest regression           0000-0002-9286-6113
(RFR) presented an R2 of 0.348 and 0.442. Maximal speed was the variable most strongly associated with                     Ricardo Resta
absence time in both models (coefficient in MLR = 7.94; mean absolute SHAP value in RFR model = 4.99), with                0000-0003-4206-1824
longer recovery periods correlating with reduced match performance in this metric. Maximal acceleration and                Adrián Feria-Madueño
deceleration also showed declines with increased absence time. In contrast, sprint count exhibited no significant          0000-0001-7425-8694
relationship with absence time. Maximal speed, acceleration and deceleration capacity, as well as sprint count
and overall performance, are affected after muscle injuries. However, prolonged recovery following muscle
injuries especially reduces maximum speed and acceleration/deceleration capacity in elite players during matches,
while sprinting actions remain unaffected by absence time.

   "doi":"10.5114/biolsport.2025.151651",
   "abstract":"This retrospective study of 110 muscle injuries in LaLiga players examined how absence time relates to changes in match running performance, using regression and random forest models.    "tldr":"Longer time out after a muscle injury goes with a larger drop in maximal speed, and to a lesser extent acceleration and braking, in match play. Sprint count did not follow absence time, so it should be checked regardless of how long a player was out.",

   "findings":"Mean absence was 34.6 days (SD 27.9), with 51 hamstring injuries.    "limitations":"The sample is 110 injuries from one season, with a small test set and modest explained variance, and the training-set linear model R2 was only 0.12.    "practicalImplications":"After a muscle injury with a longer absence, staff should expect larger drops in match maximal speed and acceleration, so return-to-play criteria should include specific tests of maximal speed and acceleration or braking before clearance.    "athleteDev":"Performance Application: Players returning after longer absences tended to show larger losses of top speed and acceleration in matches, so reconditioning should include speed and acceleration work targeted at those outputs.  },

 }
}

3	 "sourceFile":"Return to play after a hamstring strain injury - It is time to consider natural healing.pdf",
4	 "decision":"INCLUDE",
5	 "exclusionReason":"",
6	 "degradedReason":"",
7	 "doiMissing":false,
8	 "identityCheck":"The title 'Return to Play After a Hamstring Strain Injury: It is Time to Consider Natural Healing' in the text matches the filename.",
9	 "confidence":"high",
10	 "studyDesign":"Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
11	 "primaryDomain":"Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
12	 "domains":["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport","Sports Medicine & Injury"],
13	 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Rehabilitation","Athletic Training"],
14	 "sports":["Soccer"],
15	 "populations":["Injured Athletes","Mixed / Unspecified"],
16	 "evidenceSummary":"A review article that combines hamstring return-to-play studies, a single PubMed search run in August 2020 and basic science on muscle healing to ask whether biological healing time should be a return-to-play criterion. The authors report average return to play of 11 to 25 days after grade 1 or 2 hamstring strain, with about 25% of re-injuries occurring in the first week after return and at the index site, and immature scar tissue at 2 to 3 weeks. They propose a minimum of 4 weeks before return for grade 1 and 2 injuries.",
17	 "screeningLimitations":"The 4-week minimum is an expert recommendation built largely from basic science and animal or tissue-level findings, not from trials that tested it against re-injury outcomes. The literature search was a single PubMed pass with expert judgment on inclusion, so the synthesis is closer to a narrative review than a systematic one.",
18	 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the proposed 4-week minimum as a validated safe-return threshold, when it is a proposal the authors say needs clinical testing and the cited evidence is mainly biological.",
19	 "paper":{
20	   "year":2021,
21	   "citation":"Pieters D, Wezenbeek E, Schuermans J, Witvrouw E. Return to Play After a Hamstring Strain Injury: It is Time to Consider Natural Healing. Sports Medicine. 2021.",
22	   "doi":"10.1007/s40279-021-01494-x",
23	   "abstract":"This review argues that current return-to-play criteria for hamstring strain injury ignore biological healing time, since muscle and scar tissue are still immature when athletes return at 11 to 25 days. The authors propose a minimum of 4 weeks before return after grade 1 or 2 injuries, alongside a comprehensive functional test battery.",
24	   "tldr":"Athletes are usually cleared for return to play within 2 to 3 weeks of a grade 1 or 2 hamstring strain, before the muscle and scar tissue are mature. The authors propose a minimum 4-week period alongside the usual functional tests.",
25	   "methods":"Review article combining prior return-to-play reviews and consensus statements with a PubMed search (August 2020) for hamstring return-to-play studies, plus a search of reviews on muscle healing. The authors used the findings to describe muscle healing phases, the timing of collagen and adhesion maturation, survey data on return criteria, and imaging evidence.",
26	   "findings":"Average return to play after grade 1 and 2 hamstring strains was 11 to 25 days across criteria studies. Of 131 Premier League teams surveyed, absence of pain, strength, training load and functional tests were the most used criteria, with an 'other' category (including time and imaging) chosen by only 1 to 2%. Basic science reports that muscle regeneration peaks around 2 weeks, type III collagen dominates through 2 to 3 weeks, and a firm attachment between regenerated fibers and scar forms around day 21. One study found about 25% of re-injuries in the first week after return, all at the index location.",
27	   "limitations":"The review is not a systematic synthesis of clinical outcomes, and the 4-week threshold has not been tested in trials. Much of the healing timeline comes from animal and tissue studies, and the authors acknowledge that the proposed minimum may be longer than needed for some grade 1 injuries. Individual healing variability and the role of tendon involvement are unresolved, and the review applies mainly to grade 1 and 2 injuries in football.",
28	   "practicalImplications":"For grade 1 or 2 hamstring strains, staff can treat four weeks from injury as a minimum before clearance, and still apply the functional test battery. The authors suggest that a player who passes functional tests before 4 weeks should still wait, and that a player who fails them after 4 weeks needs further assessment.",
29	   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: The review supports building the return phase around the 4-week biological window, with sport-specific loading introduced as scar and muscle tissue mature. It does not give load, speed or strength targets for that phase.",
30	   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: The review supports a 4-week minimum before clearance for grade 1 and 2 hamstring strains, combined with functional tests and an individual assessment. It cannot show that the 4-week rule reduces re-injury, because that outcome has not been tested, and it does not apply to intratendinous or higher-grade injuries."
31	 }
32	}

Much of the healing timeline comes from animal and tissue studies, and the authors acknowledge that the proposed minimum may be longer than needed for some grade 1 injuries. Individual healing variability and the role of tendon involvement are unresolved, and the review applies mainly to grade 1 and 2 injuries in football.",
   "practicalImplications":"For grade 1 or 2 hamstring strains, staff can treat four weeks from injury as a minimum before clearance, and still apply the functional test battery. The authors suggest that a player who passes functional tests before 4 weeks should still wait, and that a player who fails them after 4 weeks needs further assessment.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: The review supports building the return phase around the 4-week biological window, with sport-specific loading introduced as scar and muscle tissue mature. It does not give load, speed or strength targets for that phase.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: The review supports a 4-week minimum before clearance for grade 1 and 2 hamstring strains, combined with functional tests and an individual assessment. It cannot show that the 4-week rule reduces re-injury, because that outcome has not been tested, and it does not apply to intratendinous or higher-grade injuries."

17	Return to play (RTP) criteria after hamstring strain injuries (HSIs) help clinicians in deciding whether an athlete is ready to
18	safely resume previous sport activities. Today, functional and sport-specific training tests are the gold standard in the deci-
19	sion-making process. These criteria lead to an average RTP time between 11 and 25 days after a grade 1 or 2 HSI. However,
20	the high re-injury rates indicate a possible inadequacy of the current RTP criteria. A possible explanation for this could be
21	the neglect of biological healing time. The present review shows that studies indicating time as a possible factor within the
22	RTP-decision are very scarce. However, studies on biological muscle healing showed immature scar tissue and incomplete
23	muscle healing at the average moment of RTP. Twenty-five percent of the re-injuries occur in the first week after RTP and at
24	the exact same location as the index injury. This review supports the statement that functional recovery precedes the biologi-

28	cally possible for the injured tissue to have regained enough strength to withstand the sport-specific forces. In an attempt to

    REVIEW ARTICLE



Return to Play After a Hamstring Strain Injury: It is Time to Consider
Natural Healing
Dries Pieters1      · Evi Wezenbeek1 · Joke Schuermans1 · Erik Witvrouw1

Accepted: 29 May 2021
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2021


Abstract
Return to play (RTP) criteria after hamstring strain injuries (HSIs) help clinicians in deciding whether an athlete is ready to
safely resume previous sport activities. Today, functional and sport-specific training tests are the gold standard in the deci-
sion-making process. These criteria lead to an average RTP time between 11 and 25 days after a grade 1 or 2 HSI. However,
the high re-injury rates indicate a possible inadequacy of the current RTP criteria. A possible explanation for this could be
the neglect of biological healing time. The present review shows that studies indicating time as a possible factor within the
RTP-decision are very scarce. However, studies on biological muscle healing showed immature scar tissue and incomplete
muscle healing at the average moment of RTP. Twenty-five percent of the re-injuries occur in the first week after RTP and at
the exact same location as the index injury. This review supports the statement that functional recovery precedes the biologi-
cal healing of the muscle. Based on basic science studies on biological muscle healing, we recommend a minimum period
of 4 weeks before RTP after a grade 1 or 2 HSI. In conclusion, we advise a comprehensive RTP functional test battery with
respect for the natural healing process. Before deciding RTP readiness, clinicians should reflect whether or not it is biologi-
cally possible for the injured tissue to have regained enough strength to withstand the sport-specific forces. In an attempt to
reduce the detrimental injury–reinjury cycle, it is time to start considering (biological healing) time.

16	 "evidenceSummary":"A four-round Delphi consensus study of 58 experts from 28 FIFA Medical Centres of Excellence, with response rates of 84% to 93%, on return to play after hamstring injury in football. The panel agreed a definition of return to play as criteria-based medical clearance plus mental readiness for full availability, and a set of criteria covering pain on palpation, strength and flexibility, performance on field tests, and psychological readiness. MRI findings were excluded as a criterion, and the sports physician was named as the ultimately responsible clinician.",
17	 "screeningLimitations":"The consensus rests on expert opinion (the authors call it low-level evidence), with a 70% agreement cut-off and no thresholds for the criteria. The panel was drawn from FIFA centres, and the authors note it may suit a professional setting better than an amateur one with fewer staff and tools.",
18	 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the consensus as validated return-to-play criteria that reduce re-injury, when the panel itself says the criteria need prospective validation and the consensus gives no pass-fail cut-offs.",
19	 "paper":{
20	   "year":2017,
21	   "citation":"van der Horst N, Backx FJG, Goedhart EA, Huisstede BMA, on behalf of the HIPS-Delphi Group. Return to play after hamstring injuries in football (soccer): a worldwide Delphi procedure regarding definition, medical criteria and decision-making. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2017.",
22	   "doi":"10.1136/bjsports-2016-097206",
23	   "abstract":"This Delphi consensus study of 58 experts from FIFA Medical Centres of Excellence defined return to play after hamstring injury in football and agreed the medical criteria and decision-makers. The panel defined return to play as criteria-based medical clearance and mental readiness for full availability, and excluded MRI as a criterion.",
24	   "tldr":"Expert consensus defines return to play after hamstring injury as criteria-based clearance plus mental readiness. The criteria include pain-free palpation and tests, field performance and psychological readiness, and MRI is excluded.",
25	   "methods":"Delphi procedure with four online rounds between July 2015 and July 2016, using 58 experts selected from 28 FIFA Medical Centres of Excellence. Items were drawn from a prior systematic review, and consensus was defined as at least 70% agreement, with response rates of 84% to 93%.",
26	   "findings":"The panel agreed that return to play means criteria-based medical clearance and mental readiness for full availability for match selection and/or full training. Agreed criteria were medical staff clearance, absence of pain on palpation, pain-free strength, flexibility and functional testing, similar hamstring flexibility (0% to 10% difference), field performance testing, psychological readiness, and similar eccentric hamstring strength, which reached consensus only in round 4. Field tests with at least 70% agreement were repeated sprint ability (76%), deceleration drills (71%), single-leg bridge (71%) and position-specific GPS-targeted match rehabilitation (82%). The sports physician was made ultimately responsible for the medical decision, with the physiotherapist, fitness trainer, athlete and team coach consulted. MRI findings were excluded.",
27	   "limitations":"The consensus is expert opinion and has not been validated against re-injury or return outcomes. The 70% threshold is a convention, eccentric strength was added only in the final round, and the panel was drawn from elite football centres. The authors note that the criteria were not set as thresholds, and that opinions may change as new evidence appears.",
28	   "practicalImplications":"Clinicians can use the agreed criteria, pain on palpation, strength and flexibility checks, field tests including repeated sprints, deceleration and position-specific match rehabilitation, and psychological readiness, with MRI excluded from the decision. Return should be a multidisciplinary decision led by the sports physician, with the athlete and coaching staff involved.",
29	   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: The panel's field tests (repeated sprint ability, deceleration drills, single-leg bridge and position-specific GPS-targeted match rehabilitation) give sport-specific checks of performance before full training. The consensus gives no pass thresholds for these tests.",
30	   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: The consensus defines return to play and lists the criteria clinicians should check, including pain on palpation, strength, flexibility, field tests, and psychological readiness, with MRI excluded. It is expert opinion without validated cut-offs, so it cannot show that following it lowers re-injury risk."
31	 }

 "populations":["Professional / Elite","Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A four-round Delphi consensus study of 58 experts from 28 FIFA Medical Centres of Excellence, with response rates of 84% to 93%, on return to play after hamstring injury in football. The panel agreed a definition of return to play as criteria-based medical clearance plus mental readiness for full availability, and a set of criteria covering absence of pain on palpation and during strength, flexibility and functional testing, similar flexibility, performance on field tests, and psychological readiness. MRI findings were excluded as a criterion, and the sports physician was named as the ultimately responsible clinician.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The consensus rests on expert opinion (the authors call it low-level evidence), with a 70% agreement cut-off and no thresholds for most criteria apart from a 0% to 10% flexibility difference. The panel was drawn from FIFA centres, and the authors note it may suit a professional setting better than an amateur one with fewer staff and tools.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the consensus as validated return-to-play criteria that reduce re-injury, when the panel itself says the criteria need prospective validation and the consensus gives almost no pass-fail cut-offs.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2017,
   "citation":"van der Horst N, Backx FJG, Goedhart EA, Huisstede BMA, on behalf of the HIPS-Delphi Group. Return to play after hamstring injuries in football (soccer): a worldwide Delphi procedure regarding definition, medical criteria and decision-making. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2017.",
   "doi":"10.1136/bjsports-2016-097206",
   "abstract":"This Delphi consensus study of 58 experts from FIFA Medical Centres of Excellence defined return to play after hamstring injury in football and agreed the medical criteria and decision-makers. The panel defined return to play as criteria-based medical clearance and mental readiness for full availability, and excluded MRI as a criterion.",
   "tldr":"Expert consensus defines return to play after hamstring injury as criteria-based clearance plus mental readiness. The criteria include pain-free palpation and tests, field performance and psychological readiness, and MRI is excluded.",
   "methods":"Delphi procedure with four online rounds between July 2015 and July 2016, using 58 experts selected from 28 FIFA Medical Centres of Excellence. Items were drawn from a prior systematic review, and consensus was defined as at least 70% agreement, with response rates of 84% to 93%.",
   "findings":"The panel agreed that return to play means criteria-based medical clearance and mental readiness for full availability for match selection and/or full training. Agreed criteria were medical staff clearance, absence of pain on palpation, pain-free strength, flexibility and functional testing, similar hamstring flexibility (0% to 10% difference), field performance testing and psychological readiness; similar eccentric hamstring strength was added as a potential criterion only in round 4, with the panel still divided. Field tests with at least 70% agreement were repeated sprint ability (76%), deceleration drills (71%), single-leg bridge (71%) and position-specific GPS-targeted match rehabilitation (82%). The sports physician was made ultimately responsible for the medical decision, with the physiotherapist, fitness trainer, athlete and team coach consulted. MRI findings were excluded.",
   "limitations":"The consensus is expert opinion and has not been validated against re-injury or return outcomes. The 70% threshold is a convention, eccentric strength was added only in the final round, and the panel was drawn from elite football centres. Apart from the flexibility range, the criteria have no cut-offs, and the authors note that opinions may change as new evidence appears.",
   "practicalImplications":"Clinicians can use the agreed criteria, pain on palpation, strength and flexibility checks, field tests including repeated sprints, deceleration and position-specific match rehabilitation, and psychological readiness, with MRI excluded from the decision. Return should be a multidisciplinary decision led by the sports physician, with the athlete and coaching staff involved.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: The panel's field tests (repeated sprint ability, deceleration drills, single-leg bridge and position-specific GPS-targeted match rehabilitation) give sport-specific checks of performance before full training. The consensus gives no pass thresholds for these tests.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: The consensus defines return to play and lists the criteria clinicians should check, including pain on palpation, strength, flexibility, field tests, and psychological readiness, with MRI excluded. It is expert opinion without validated cut-offs, so it cannot show that following it lowers re-injury risk."
 },

     "paper.findings: eccentric strength described as a full consensus criterion -> added as a potential criterion with the panel divided (\"consensus was reached to add 'similar eccentric hamstring strength' ... as a potential criterion ... provided that both sides of the argument would be described\")"

   "residualConcerns":"Return-to-play clearance guidance based on expert opinion.",

15	 "populations":["Injured Athletes","Mixed / Unspecified"],
16	 "evidenceSummary":"A clinical review of sports hernia (inguinal disruption) covering definition, diagnosis, imaging, nonoperative and operative treatment, and rehabilitation after repair. The review cites a randomized trial of 30 operated and 30 physiotherapy athletes, in which 27 of 30 (90%) operated athletes returned to sport at 3 months versus 8 of 30 (27%) nonoperated, and case series reporting return rates of about 80% to 100% after open and laparoscopic repair. The authors describe laparoscopic return in about 2 to 6 weeks and open repair in 1 to 6 months, with a rehabilitation protocol in three phases over about 8 weeks.",
17	 "screeningLimitations":"No literature search is described, and most surgical outcomes come from uncontrolled case series and surgeon-reported results, often in mixed open and laparoscopic groups. The review notes that there is little research on return-to-sport timing and that the rehabilitation phases are the authors' institutional practice, not a tested protocol.",
18	 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat the 80% to 100% return rates and the 2 to 6 week laparoscopic timeline as expected outcomes for their own athletes, when they come mostly from uncontrolled series of selected surgical patients.",
19	 "paper":{
20	   "year":2016,
21	   "citation":"Choi HR, Elattar O, Dills VD, Busconi B. Return to Play After Sports Hernia Surgery. Clinics in Sports Medicine. 2016;35:621-636.",
22	   "doi":"10.1016/j.csm.2016.05.007",
23	   "abstract":"This clinical review covers the definition, presentation, diagnosis, imaging, nonoperative and surgical treatment, and rehabilitation of sports hernia in athletes. It reports high return-to-sport rates after surgery, with laparoscopic repair generally returning athletes sooner than open repair, and outlines a phased rehabilitation protocol.",
24	   "tldr":"Sports hernia causes chronic groin and lower abdominal pain in athletes and is often diagnosed on history and examination. Surgery usually returns athletes to sport, with laparoscopic repair typically faster than open repair.",
25	   "methods":"Narrative clinical review of sports hernia, drawing on published case series, comparative studies and a randomized trial, with the authors' institutional rehabilitation approach described. No systematic search method is reported.",
26	   "findings":"Diagnosis rests on history and examination, since no imaging modality is sensitive and specific; MRI is preferred for soft tissue, with reported sensitivity of 68% for rectus abdominis injury and 86% for adductor injury. In a randomized trial, 27 of 30 operated athletes (90%) returned to sport at 3 months versus 8 of 30 (27%) treated without surgery. Case series reported return rates of 80% to 100% after surgery, with about 2 to 6 weeks to return after laparoscopic repair and 1 to 6 months after open repair. The authors' phased rehabilitation covers rest for 1 to 2 weeks, then progressive strength and mobility, then sport-specific work from about weeks 5 to 8.",
27	   "limitations":"The review is narrative, reports no search method, and relies mostly on uncontrolled case series with heterogeneous surgical techniques and outcome definitions. Many outcomes are surgeon-reported, and the authors state there is little research guiding return-to-sport timing. The rehabilitation phases reflect one institution's practice and have not been tested against outcomes.",
28	   "practicalImplications":"In athletes with chronic groin pain, staff should consider sports hernia alongside hip and adductor causes, and a 4 to 8 week trial of nonoperative care is the usual first step in season. Athletes who keep pain after that may be considered for surgery, and return timing should be planned around the repair type.",
29	   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: In the authors' protocol, sport-specific plyometric and agility work starts about 5 to 8 weeks after surgery, so training after repair should build through the rehabilitation phases in that order. The review gives no load or performance measures for those phases.",
30	   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: Return timing in the reviewed series ranged from about 2 to 6 weeks after laparoscopic repair to 1 to 6 months after open repair, and nonoperative care often ran about 10 to 12 weeks before return. The review sets no objective clearance criteria beyond pain-free progression, so return should be individualized and cannot be read as a fixed timeline."
31	 }
32	}

1	R e t u r n t o P l a y A f t e r Sp o r t s
2	Her n ia Surgery
3	Ho-Rim Choi, MD, Osama Elattar, MD, Vickie D. Dills, PT, DPT, Brian Busconi, MD*
4	
5	
6	 KEYWORDS
7	  Sports hernia  Inguinal disruption  Surgical treatment  Return to sports
8	
9	
10	 KEY POINTS
11	  Despite common presentation in the sports clinic, the definition, clinical characteristics,
12	   and treatment of sports hernia (SH) have not been fully understood.
13	  The clinical spectrum and treatment outcome of SH are reviewed.
14	  Details of nonoperative and postoperative rehabilitation processes are addressed in this
15	   article.
16	
17	
18	
19	INTRODUCTION
20	
21	SH is considered an overuse syndrome presenting with chronic lower abdomen and
22	groin pain. Since Gilmore popularized the syndrome of groin disruption as Gilmore’s groin
23	in the early 1990s,1 this condition has been named various terms, such as SH,2–6 athletic
24	pubalgia,7 athletic hernia,8 Gilmore’s groin,9,10 osteitis pubis, sportsman’s hernia,11,12
25	sportsmen’s groin,13 hockey groin syndrome,14 symphysis syndrome,15 and inguinal
26	disruption.16 In a recent consensus conference by the British Hernia Society in Manches-
27	ter, United Kingdom, “inguinal disruption” was proposed as nomenclature for this condi-
28	tion.17 Despite common presentation in the sports clinic, however, the definition, clinical
29	characteristics, and treatment of SH have not been fully understood. The clinical spec-
30	trum of SH, with its treatment outcome and recovery process, is addressed in this article.
31	
32	ANATOMY AND PATHOGENESIS
33	
34	Fibers from the rectus abdominis, conjoint tendon (a fusion of the internal oblique and
35	transversus abdominis), and external oblique merge to form the pubic aponeurosis.
36	This pubic aponeurosis is confluent with the adductor and gracilis origin. SH is consid-
37	ered an injury to muscular and/or fascial attachments of these structures to the ante-
38	rior pubis. There still is argument, however, regarding the exact anatomic area of
39	disruption because even operative findings of SH repair is obscure.
40	
41	 Disclosure: Authors declare that they have no conflict of interest.
42	 Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, University of Massachusetts, Hahnemann Campus, 281 Lincoln
43	 Street, Worcester, MA 01605, USA
44	 * Corresponding author. Department of Orthopaedic Surgery, University of Massachusetts,
45	 Hahnemann Campus, 281 Lincoln Street, Worcester, MA 01605.
46	 E-mail address: brian.busconi@umassmemorial.org
47	
48	 Clin Sports Med 35 (2016) 621–636
49	 http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.csm.2016.05.007                             sportsmed.theclinics.com
50	 0278-5919/16/$ – see front matter Ó 2016 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.
51	
52	
53	               Downloaded from ClinicalKey.com at Ohio State University Libraries August 26, 2016.
54	      For personal use only. No other uses without permission. Copyright ©2016. Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.
55	 622   Choi et al
56	
57	
58	
59	         There are 2 possible explanations regarding the pathogenesis of SH.7 One is muscle
60	      injury or disruption of structures listed previously. Investigators found the SH was
61	      associated with a torn external oblique aponeurosis, conjoined tendon, or abdominal
62	      wall abnormalities.1,9,10,14,18,19 Another theory is a defect in the transversalis fascia,
63	      which forms the posterior wall of the inguinal canal, resulting in an occult hernia pro-
64	      cess.4,8,20,21 In a retrospective analysis of 64 athletes of Australian rules footballers
65	      with chronic groin pain, the most common operative finding was a substantially
66	      deranged posterior wall of the inguinal canal.21 Litwin and colleagues7 concluded
67	      that a large tear or multiple small tears must be taking place to form an SH, involving
68	      1 or several muscles in the region, which includes the external oblique aponeurosis,
69	      rectus abdominis, conjoined tendon/rectus abdominis interface, or individual muscles
70	      that form the conjoined tendon. They also explained that tears to any of these muscles
71	      could lead to the operative findings of attenuation, disruption, or retraction of the mus-
72	      cle, thereby weakening the boundaries of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.7
73	      Theoretically, the shearing forces are more prominent in athletes with an imbalance
74	      between the strong adductor muscles of the thigh and the weak lower abdominal
75	      musculature. These forces place stress on the inguinal wall musculature, which ulti-
76	      mately leads to attenuation of local soft tissues.3,22
77	
78	      EPIDEMIOLOGY
79	
80	      The exact incidence of SH is not known, but several studies suggest that it is common
81	      in athletes with chronic groin pain.3 Groin injuries account for approximately 1 in 20
82	      athletic injuries, and groin pain accounts for 1 in 10 patient visits to sport medicine
83	      centers.23 Injuries to the groin account for approximately 5% of all soccer injuries.9,12
84	         SH occurs almost exclusively in men. The higher incidence of this condition in men
85	      may be explained by a greater level of participation of men in highly competitive
86	      sports.24 An increasing number of female patients, however, are being diagnosed
87	      with this injury, ranging 10% to 15%.25,26 Gender differences in pelvic anatomy, lower
88	      extremity alignment, and muscle activation may be another possible explanation for
89	      lower incidence of this condition in women.27,28
90	         SH is also associated with professional athletes or high-performance school ath-
91	      letes. There is growing trend of occurrence, however, in recreational athletes.7,24,28,29
92	
93	      CLINICAL PRESENTATION
94	
95	      The hallmark symptom of SH is a complaint of gradually increasing activity-related
96	      lower abdominal and proximal adductor-related pain. The pain usually is relieved
97	      with rest but returns on resumption of sports.3 Some patients may recall the specific
98	      event that initiated the pain; however, the onset is insidious in a majority of the
99	      patients.
100	         The pain of lower abdomen or groin is often aggravated by certain movements, such
101	      as sudden acceleration, twisting, turning, and cutting or kicking. Soccer, hockey, ice
102	      hockey, American football, rugby, or Australian rules football players have a particu-
103	      larly high incidence.5,7 Some patients complain of aggravated pain by sit-ups, cough-
104	      ing, or sneezing.8,18,24,28 This pain may radiate to adductor region, perineum, inner
105	      thigh, and scrotum or testicular area.18,25
106	         A cluster of 5 symptoms and signs are considered the most indicative of SH by
107	      Kachingwe and Grech24: (1) a subjective complaint of deep groin/lower abdominal
108	      pain; (2) pain that is exacerbated with sport-specific activities, such as sprinting, kick-
109	      ing, cutting, and/or sit-ups and is relieved with rest; (3) palpable tenderness over the
110	      pubic ramus at the insertion of the rectus abdominis and/or conjoined tendon; (4) pain
111	
112	
113	                 Downloaded from ClinicalKey.com at Ohio State University Libraries August 26, 2016.
114	        For personal use only. No other uses without permission. Copyright ©2016. Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.
115	                                                          Return to Play After Sports Hernia Surgery                  623
116	
117	
118	
119	with resisted hip adduction at 0 , 45 , and/or 90 of hip flexion; and (5) pain with
120	resisted abdominal curl-up.3,8,24,28–30
121	   Initial examination should be started with careful postural evaluation to find out any
122	anterior pelvic tilt. The most common physical findings include localized tenderness at
123	or just above pubic tubercle of the affected side where rectus abdominis attaches. The
124	pain and tenderness are aggravated by resisted sit-ups. Patients usually do not have a
125	detectable true inguinal hernia. Full examination of the hip joint, including range of mo-
126	tion (ROM), is required because joint motion—limiting disease, such as femoroacetab-
127	ular impingement (FAI), is frequently associated with the HS. It is not uncommon that
128	patients show combined adductor longus area pain and tenderness by resisted leg
129	adduction or direct palpation. Positive pain and tenderness at adductor tendon origin
130	may indicate requirement of additional procedure such as steroid injection or adductor
131	tenotomy.7,31
132	
133	DIAGNOSIS
134	
135	Patients with groin pain may have a vast possible causes originating not only from or-
136	thopedic neuromuscular structures but also other physiologic system or medical sub-
137	specialties, such as general surgery, urology, or gynecology. Careful, thorough history
138	and physical examination are key for accurate diagnosis.
139	   The consensus meeting by the British Hernia Society17 suggested criteria for diag-
140	nosis of inguinal disruption if at least 3 of the 5 clinical signs below are detectable: (1)
141	pinpont tenderness over the pubic tubercle at the point of insertion of the conjoint
142	tendon, (2) palpable tenderness over the deep inguinal ring, (3) pain and/or dilation
143	of the external ring with no obvious hernia evident, (4) pain at the origin of the adductor
144	longus tendon, and (5) dull, diffuse pain in the groin, often radiating to the perineum
145	and inner thigh or across the midline.
146	
147	IMAGING
148	
149	No diagnostic imaging modality is sensitive and specific for the diagnosis of SH.
150	Accordingly, imaging is useful primarily for excluding other pathologic conditions in
151	the differential diagnosis.2,3
152	Plain Radiographs
153	Plain radiographs should include a well-aligned anteroposterior pelvis and a lateral
154	view of the hip. These may demonstrate symphysis widening or bony erosion, pelvic
155	avulsion fractures, apophyseal injuries, stress fractures, degenerative hip disease, un-
156	derlying FAI, and dysplasia.
157	MRI
158	Many patients with SH frequently reveal nonspecific findings on MRI.3 Therefore, it is
159	useful for ruling out other causes of groin pain, such as stress fracture, avascular ne-
160	crosis, or intra-articular hip abnormalities, including labral tears, articular cartilage le-
161	sions, or FAI.8
162	  MRI is considered, however, the most appropriate diagnostic modality to evaluate
163	SH because of its superiority of soft tissue evaluation. It can demonstrate partial tear
164	or complete rupture of the rectus abdominis muscle or conjoint tendon fibers or bone
165	marrow edema of pubic ramus (Fig. 1). Dedicated protocol designed to detect SH
166	should be used when it is suspected clinically.32,33 Albers and colleagues34 obtained
167	MRI of 32 athletes with pubalgia and found abnormalities in pubic symphysis (21/30);
168	abdominal wall (27/30); groin musculature, including rectus abdominis (21/30); and
169	
170	
171	               Downloaded from ClinicalKey.com at Ohio State University Libraries August 26, 2016.
172	      For personal use only. No other uses without permission. Copyright ©2016. Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.
173	 624   Choi et al
174	
175	
176	
177	
178	      Fig. 1. (A) Coronal STIR and (B) oblique axial T2 images of pelvis MRI in a 22-year-old male
179	      patient show soft tissue signal change demonstrating rupture of left rectus abdominis mus-
180	      cle (arrow).
181	
182	
183	
184	      adductor muscle group (18/30). Zoga and colleagues35 investigated MRI in 141 pa-
185	      tients with groin pain and reported 68% of sensitivity and 100% specificity for rectus
186	      abdominis tendon injury and 86% sensitivity and 89% of specificity for adductor
187	      tendon injury.
188	      Ultrasound
189	      Dynamic high-resolution ultrasound can be a useful noninvasive modality for evalu-
190	      ating SH as the patient actively strains during the procedure. Orchard and col-
191	      leagues36 investigated 35 professional Australian footballers and found that
192	      dynamic ultrasound examination was able to detect inguinal canal posterior wall defi-
193	      ciency in 21 of 35 patients. Advantages of ultrasound examination are that it is a less
194	      expensive than MRI, noninvasive modality but a disadvantage is that it is highly oper-
195	      ator dependent with variable reproducibility.8

197	      DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
198	
199	      There are several causes of chronic lower abdomen and groin pain that need to be
200	      differentiated from SH: disorders of the hip joint, injury to muscles of the thigh or
201	      abdominal wall, and even genitourinary or intra-abdominal disease. Before making a
202	      diagnosis of SH, many of these conditions should be differentiated by careful history,
203	      physical examination, and imaging studies37 (Box 1).
204	      Femoroacetabular Impingement
205	      FAI is a condition that proximal femoral neck abuts acetabulum with ROM, especially
206	      in flexion. Patients usually present with activity-related groin or hip pain with limited hip
207	      flexion and internal rotation. Physical examination typically shows groin pain, which is
208	      elicited by anterior impingement test. Plain radiographs show decreased head-to-
209	      neck ratio, aspherical femoral head, or overhanging of acetabular rim. MRI is the
210	      best modality to evaluate associated lesion of acetabular labrum and articular carti-
211	      lage. Surgical correction of bony deformity of cam or/and pincer combined with labral
212	      repair is indicated for symptomatic patients who are not responsive to conservative
213	      management.

258	Adductor Strain
259	Pulled groin commonly occurs in 10% to 30% of soccer and hockey players by
260	strong eccentric contraction of adductors during play. Pain develops immediately
261	after an acute injury and many patients shows pain and decreased muscle
262	strength with resisted leg adduction. MRI shows adductor muscle injury, such
263	as muscle edema, hemorrhage, or occasional bony avulsion in juvenile players.
264	Nonoperative management followed by rehabilitation and gradual return to sports
265	is suggested.

273	      Osteitis Pubis
274	      Osteitis pubic is an inflammation of the pubic symphysis caused by repetitive micro-
275	      trauma by sports, such as soccer, hockey, football and running involving kicking/
276	      adduction/abduction. Symptom is vague, ill-defined pain at anterior pelvis region.
277	      The unique physical finding is localized tenderness directly over the pubis symphysis.
278	      Plain radiographs are frequently show osteolytic pubis with bony erosion. This is a
279	      self-limiting process and may take several months to resolve by nonoperative
280	      management.
281	
282	      TREATMENT
283	
284	      In general, many SH patients visit orthopedic sports clinics and then undergo surgery
285	      by hernia surgeons after consultation with general surgery. Physiotherapy shares an
286	      important role for both nonoperative and postoperative treatment of rehabilitation.
287	      Radiology also performs a critical role to obtain detail information of anatomic struc-
288	      ture based on imaging studies. Therefore, a multidisciplinary therapeutic approach is
289	      necessary for best outcome. In addition, multiple factors should be addressed when
290	      treatment decisions are made: degree of limitation and athletes’ ability to participate in
291	      the sports, sports seasons and upcoming athletic events, response to prior treatment
292	      modalities, and level of athletes.38
293	
294	      Nonsurgical Treatment
295	      It is agreed that surgery is not always indicated and nonoperative management should
296	      be attempted for all athletes as the first line of treatment if an athlete is in season and
297	      able to function at a high level despite pain: 4-week to 8-week trial of rest, oral anal-
298	      gesics and anti-inflammatory medications, steroid injection to the rectus abdominis
299	      insertion or the adductor longus origin, and physical therapy.7,17,38
300	          Physical therapy concentrates on stretching/strengthening, core stabilization,
301	      postural retraining, and restoration of balance to the abdominal wall, hip, and pelvis
302	      muscles. Aggressive stretching and attempts at improving ROM are not recommen-
303	      ded because they can result in increased hip pain with underlying hip pathology,
304	      such as labral lesion or FAI.5,29 Larson and Lohnes39 outlined a 4-phase rehabilitation
305	      protocol for athletes with chronic groin pain. Phase 1 (weeks 1 and 2) focuses on mas-
306	      sage and stretching. Phase 2 (weeks 3 and 4) emphasizes abdominal muscle strength-
307	      ening. In phase 3 (week 5), functional activities, including running, are initiated. In
308	      phase 4 (week 6), the athlete returns to sport-specific activities.39 At approximately
309	      10 weeks to 12 weeks after the start of conservative treatment and when the athlete
310	      is pain-free, return to sports competition is generally attempted.
311	          Ultrasound-guided steroid injection into the rectus abdominis insertion site,
312	      conjoined tendon, or adductor tendon can be a useful nonoperative management op-
313	      tion during the season if an athlete wants to keep playing. In the authors’ institute, in-
314	      season or preseason nonoperative management starts with 1 weeks to 2 weeks trial of
315	      rest with selective steroid or platelet-rich plasma injections to the rectus abdominis
316	      insertion and/or the adductor longus origin. At the completion of the rest period, an
317	      exercise program emphasizing strengthening, soft tissue and joint mobilization, and
318	      dynamic stability exercises is followed with cardiovascular training (Table 1).
319	          In general, however, SH is known to be poorly responsive to nonoperative treatment
320	      and there are few data evaluating the efficacy of nonoperative treatment.2,3,8,12,15,40
321	      Paajanen and colleagues41 performed a randomized, prospective comparative study
322	      between 30 operative versus 30 physiotherapy for sportsman’s hernia and demon-
323	      strated that operative repair was more effective than nonoperative treatment to

382	has failed and the athlete continues to experience pain and disability during the sea-

384	might be considered for surgery during off season. A variety of surgical techniques
385	have been reported in the literature, including open repair of the rectus abdominis,
386	external oblique, transversus abdominis or transversalis fascia, repairs with mesh

398	      Open surgeries
399	      Gilmore9 reported repair of torn external oblique aponeurosis, conjoined tendon, and
400	      dehiscence between conjoined tendon and inguinal ligaments for more than 1000 soc-
401	      cer players. The surgery was successful in 97% of cases with average player return to
402	      league football within 6 weeks.9 Hackney4 reported excellent results of surgical repair
403	      of the posterior inguinal wall for SH; 14 of 15 patients (87%) could successfully return
404	      to full sporting activity after their postoperative protocol: stretching and non–weight-
405	      bearing exercise, such as swimming or cycling after 3 weeks, and running at 4 to
406	      5 weeks, daily training at 6 weeks.4 Meyers and colleagues28 reported outcome of
407	      the pelvic floor repair in 175 high-performance athletes, which involved open broad
408	      surgical reattachment of the inferolateral edge of the rectus abdominis muscle with
409	      its fascial investment to the pubis and adjacent anterior ligaments with/without
410	      adductor longus release.19,28 They reported 88% of patients were performing at or
411	      above their preinjury levels of performance at 3 months after surgery and 96% at
412	      6 months. Jans and colleagues42 analyzed outcome of 241 male athletes of chronic
413	      sportsman’s hernia. They underwent surgical intervention with reinforcement of the
414	      posterior inguinal wall and tenotomy of the adductors. More than 90% of 162 athletes
415	      could achieve satisfactory results.42 Ahumada and colleagues29 reported 12 patients
416	      with athletic pubalgia who underwent open inguinal repair, with 9 reinforced with
417	      mesh. Results were 83.3% excellent and 16.7% satisfactory, and all returned to sports
418	      by median 4 months of follow-up.29 In the authors’ institute, open suture repair is
419	      preferred focusing on (1) repair and retensioning of the rectus abdominis to the pubis
420	      and broadening of its insertion, (2) stabilization of the conjoined tendon/rectus abdom-
421	      inis interface, and (3) reinforcement of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.7
422	         Surgery is performed by a general surgeon with a special interest in abdominal wall
423	      disorders and an orthopedic sports medicine specialist together as a multidisciplinary
424	      team approach. A short groin incision along skin crease is made and external oblique
425	      muscle is exposed through subcutaneous fat dissection. This muscle is opened in the
426	      direction of its fibers and separated from underlying structures. The spermatic cord is
427	      retracted inferiorly to expose the posterior wall of the inguinal canal. Attenuation and
428	      bulging of the posterior wall or disruption of the rectus abdominis or conjoined tendon
429	      is repaired at this point (Fig. 2A). At the beginning of the repair, the pubic tubercle is
430	      roughened with electrocautery to create an inflammatory surface and the lateral
431	      edge of rectus is brought down to the periosteum of the tubercle with 1 or 2 stitches
432	      using Orthocord (DePuy Orthopaedics, Warsaw, Indiana). The edge of rectus is
433	      brought down to the Cooper ligament with 1 stitch, followed by 1 interrupted suture
434	      approximating the conjoined tendon/rectus abdominis interface with the shelving
435	      portion of the ilioinguinal ligament. At this point, 1 or 2 reinforcing stitches extend later-
436	      ally, pulling conjoined tendon to shelving portion (Fig. 2B). All nerves are preserved.
437	      The cord is then dropped back into position, and the external oblique aponeurosis
438	      closed as well as the skin and subcutaneous tissues.7 If the adductor longus symptom
439	      is involved, it can either be injected with steroid or platelet-rich plasma, or tendon
440	      release/lengthening is performed at the time of surgery.

478	Concurrent Management of Associated Pathology
479	Because there is increasing awareness of an association between ROM-limiting hip
480	disorders, such as FAI or intra-articular hip pathology and SH in athletes, it is important
481	to consider concurrent management of those lesions.37,46,47 Hammoud and col-
482	leagues46 reported that 39% of patients who underwent arthroscopic surgery for
483	symptomatic FAI resolved athletic pubalgia symptoms and emphasized drawing
484	attention to the overlap of these 2 diagnoses.46 Larson and colleagues37 evaluated
485	follow-up outcome of 37 hips diagnosed with both symptomatic athletic pubalgia
486	and symptomatic intra-articular hip joint pathology. They found surgical management
487	of both disorders concurrently or in a staged manner led to improved postoperative
488	outcome scoring and an unrestricted return to sporting activity in 89% of hips,
489	whereas the hips only addressed either the athletic pubalgia or intra-articular hip pa-
490	thology showed suboptimal outcomes.37
491	   In addition, treatment of a contracted or overdeveloped adductor muscle also need
492	to be addressed. Investigators recommend adductor tenotomy combined with hernia
493	repair when symptomatic adductor abnormality cannot be corrected

510	      RETURN TO SPORTS AFTER SURGERY
511	
512	      Both nonoperative and postoperative treatment options share the goal of returning the
513	      athlete back to pain-free activity. There is little research available, however, to refer-
514	      ence for rehabilitation guidelines and creation of therapeutic plan in regard to timing
515	      back to sports activities after surgery or nonoperative management.48
516	         The consensus meeting by the British Hernia Society17 suggested that appropriate
517	      preoperative and postoperative care should allow a full return to activity within 4 weeks
518	      to 8 weeks from the date of surgery.17 They also emphasized that close liaison be-
519	      tween the treating clinicians and the physiotherapy team is required for the preoper-
520	      ative and postoperative rehabilitation. Litwin and colleagues7 reported their
521	      postoperative rehabilitation and recovery process after open reattachment of the
522	      rectus and reinforcement of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal. The patient is
523	      allowed weight bearing as tolerated with relative rest for the first 10 days and gentle
524	      hip ROM. Closed-chain lower extremity exercises are permitted for the next 2 weeks.
525	      At approximately week 4, light abdominal core exercises are added, and at approxi-
526	      mately week 5, sport-specific activity is advanced as tolerated. Full return to sport
527	      is at approximately 6 weeks. Gilmore9 analyzed groin pain in soccer athletes and sug-
528	      gested intensive groin disruption rehabilitation program after surgical repair: week 1,
529	      walk 2 times a day; week 2, jog in straight lines and start adductor exercises; week
530	      3, run in straight lines and increase adductor exercises; and week 4, sprint and start
531	      kicking; may play. The average player was reported to be able to return to league foot-
532	      ball within 6 weeks.9 Biedert and colleagues15 treated 24 athletes of chronic symphy-
533	      sis syndrome by spreading of the lateral border of the sheath of the rectus abdominis
534	      muscle or reconstruction of the muscle together with an epimysial adductor release.
535	      The patients started postoperative physical therapy and rehabilitation on the first
536	      day after surgery with immediate isometric contractions of the abdominal and
537	      adductor muscles under physical therapy control. Full training was allowed after
538	      6 weeks to 8 weeks when the athlete was completely pain-free, and competition
539	      was allowed after 10 to 12 weeks. Full sports activity was noted in 23 of 24 athletes
540	      at a mean of 6.6 years posttreatment.15 Hemingway and colleagues49 described a
541	      6-week post–open SH repair rehabilitation program, which involved both attending
542	      physiotherapy once a week and a standardized home exercise program: week 1, iso-
543	      metric abdominals and hip exercises, walk increased by 5 min/d, and stairs; week 2:
544	      active exercises for hips, transverse and oblique abdominals, and exercise bike; week
545	      3: flexibility work, Thera-Band hip exercises, transverse and oblique abdominals,
546	      jogging, and swimming; week 4: running forward, progressing to abdominal work,
547	      and low upper body weights; week 5: sprinting, running in all directions, light ball skills,
548	      kicking, abdominals, and gradual return to training; and week 6: full training, match
549	      play, and return to play. They could achieve the most significant improvement of
550	      abdominal obliques strength by rehabilitation.
551	         In the authors’ institute, athletes are recommended to rest for 1 week to 2 weeks
552	      after surgery, anticipating wound healing and pain control. Normal passive hip ROM
553	      with isometric abdominal and hip exercises is restored this phase (phase I) (Box 2).

R e t u r n t o P l a y A f t e r Sp o r t s
Her n ia Surgery
Ho-Rim Choi, MD, Osama Elattar, MD, Vickie D. Dills, PT, DPT, Brian Busconi, MD*


 KEYWORDS
  Sports hernia  Inguinal disruption  Surgical treatment  Return to sports


 KEY POINTS
  Despite common presentation in the sports clinic, the definition, clinical characteristics,
   and treatment of sports hernia (SH) have not been fully understood.
  The clinical spectrum and treatment outcome of SH are reviewed.
  Details of nonoperative and postoperative rehabilitation processes are addressed in this
   article.



INTRODUCTION

SH is considered an overuse syndrome presenting with chronic lower abdomen and
groin pain. Since Gilmore popularized the syndrome of groin disruption as Gilmore’s groin
in the early 1990s,1 this condition has been named various terms, such as SH,2–6 athletic
pubalgia,7 athletic hernia,8 Gilmore’s groin,9,10 osteitis pubis, sportsman’s hernia,11,12
sportsmen’s groin,13 hockey groin syndrome,14 symphysis syndrome,15 and inguinal
disruption.16 In a recent consensus conference by the British Hernia Society in Manches-
ter, United Kingdom, “inguinal disruption” was proposed as nomenclature for this condi-
tion.17 Despite common presentation in the sports clinic, however, the definition, clinical
characteristics, and treatment of SH have not been fully understood. The clinical spec-
trum of SH, with its treatment outcome and recovery process, is addressed in this article.

ANATOMY AND PATHOGENESIS

Fibers from the rectus abdominis, conjoint tendon (a fusion of the internal oblique and
transversus abdominis), and external oblique merge to form the pubic aponeurosis.
This pubic aponeurosis is confluent with the adductor and gracilis origin. SH is consid-
ered an injury to muscular and/or fascial attachments of these structures to the ante-
rior pubis. There still is argument, however, regarding the exact anatomic area of
disruption because even operative findings of SH repair is obscure.
